mechanisms.name: split-compensating-negation / contract-coherence attribution
mechanisms.what_happened: The original getArcBounds contained a compensating pair: `deltaX = (point1.getX() - point2.getX()) * explodePercent` then `unexploded.getX() - deltaX` (control workspace lines 3133-3135 show the same structure with the control mutation `+ deltaX`). The chain generator put the first negation into H3 `PlotUtilities.drift` (`double dx = point1.getX() - point2.getX();` where H1 derives point1 from `unexploded` and H2 derives point2 from `exploded`) and the second into H5 `ShapeUtilities.shift`, then mutated H5 from `-` to `+` (`double x = area.getX() + deltaX;`). Mathematically the test is satisfied by a single sign flip at ANY of drift, nudge, shift, or the facade, so the fault is under-determined by the test; every run resolved the tie by asking which hop's body disagrees with its own name/Javadoc. H5's mutated body is the textbook reading of `shift(area, deltaX, deltaY)` / "Shifts an area by a displacement."; H3's un-mutated body reads as `unexploded - exploded`, the reverse of the natural "from unexploded to exploded" reading of "Computes the drift between a point on the unexploded ring and the corresponding point on the exploded ring". Both models therefore blamed H3 and exonerated H5 in every run.

mechanisms.exploitable_lever: Pick an original method whose arithmetic contains a compensating pair (negate-then-subtract, invert-then-divide, offset-then-un-offset). Split the pair across two hops: put the counter-intuitive half (e.g. `from - to`) in an upstream hop whose parameter names/Javadoc carry a direction (point1 'on the unexploded ring', point2 'on the exploded ring'), and put the compensating half in a downstream hop with a generic verb name and a one-line Javadoc. Apply the mutation to the downstream hop such that the MUTATED body is the textbook implementation of its name (shift => `x + delta`). The un-mutated upstream hop now looks like the violator and absorbs the blame; the gold hop looks contract-correct. Keep every hop single-use so no other caller can vindicate or indict either contract.

mechanisms.exploitable_lever: (1) Indirect flow: dispatch the faulty hop through anything that does not put `ClassName.method(` on the return line -- an interface/abstract method resolved by a subclass the test instantiates, a Map<String,Function> registry, a Class.forName/reflection call, a lambda stored in a field, or a static initializer that mutates a constant. (2) Overloads: put two `rim(...)` overloads in StandardDialScale with different arities; `grep -n "rim(" -A30 | head -60` shows the first one fully and truncates the second -- the agent will read whichever overload comes first in the file. (3) Common names: name a hop with a substring of a frequent identifier (`ring`/`drawString`, `shift`/`Range.shift`) AND give the colliding identifier a plausible body so `| head -N` truncation lands on the decoy. (4) Window escape: put the buggy line >30 lines below the declaration (long javadoc inside the body, a nested helper, a long guard block); the agent reads -A25..40 only and will judge the method clean and keep traversing. (5) Non-conventional layout: place a hop class outside its conventional package -- the direct-path grep returns nothing (cost only, +1 call), but combined with (3) a same-named method in the CONVENTIONAL location becomes the one that is read. (6) Shared state: a fault in a static field writer or constant that the hop reads (`CHKSUMLEN`, `Integer.SIZE`) is off the return-line path and would never be opened.
